title: What Would It Take To Say We Found Life? We Asked a NASA Expert
summary: A NASA scientist answers the "podium test": what evidence would let a scientist stand before the world and say life has been found beyond Earth. The answer is a sequence of checks (is the signal real, is it contamination, could anything other than life make it) followed by independent lines of evidence and scrutiny by the whole scientific community.

chapters.title: The search for subtle signs
speakers: NASA scientist (name not in the captions)
chapters.summary: Sets up the podium test. The bar is high, and the first evidence is likely to be subtle chemistry rather than a skeleton or a technology signature.

chapters.title: Contextualizing the search
chapters.summary: What we see depends on where we look: ancient, degraded samples on Mars; tiny samples from the ocean worlds Europa and Enceladus; planet-scale signs such as an oxygenated atmosphere for exoplanets.

chapters.title: Verifying signals
chapters.summary: General principles: first make sure the signal is real, and treat life as the hypothesis of last resort.

chapters.title: Ruling out contamination
chapters.summary: Instruments are built on a planet full of life, so Earth contamination must be excluded, then whether life could live there, then every non-living process that could make the same signal.

chapters.title: Community scrutiny
chapters.summary: Independent lines of evidence build confidence, and the claim stands only after the whole scientific community has examined it.

points.text: Frame the claim as a test: what would it take to stand before an international audience and say it?
points.quote: We call this the podium test
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: The first evidence is expected to be subtle, such as chemistry, not an obvious structure.
points.quote: a lot of the evidence that we might encounter first will be much more subtle
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Chemical signs of life have to stand out above non-living (abiotic) chemistry.
points.quote: detected above a background of abiotic chemistry
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: On Mars the samples may be billions of years old, and such evidence is often degraded.
points.quote: the evidence of life is often degraded and difficult to detect
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Europa and Enceladus could hold life that is still alive (extant life).
points.quote: the tantalizing possibility of extant life
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: For exoplanets, only planet-scale changes are visible through a telescope.
points.quote: the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere or changes in surface color
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Check one: are we sure we are seeing what we think we are seeing?
points.quote: Are we sure we're seeing what we think we're seeing
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Carl Sagan's rule, quoted by the speaker: rule out every alternative first.
points.quote: life is the hypothesis of last resort
points.speaker: NASA scientist, quoting Carl Sagan

points.text: Check two: rule out contamination from the Earth-built spacecraft and instruments.
points.quote: not evidence of our own life, but evidence of indigenous life
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Check three: could anything other than life make the same thing, including processes not yet known?
points.quote: is there any other way than life to make that thing
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: Look for separate, independent lines of evidence that corroborate the first one.
points.quote: do we have separate independent lines of evidence
points.speaker: NASA scientist

points.text: The operative word is "we": the claim is made by the whole scientific community.
points.quote: the really operative word in our question is we
points.speaker: NASA scientist

actions.text: When you evaluate a bold claim in your own field, run the same three checks in order: is the signal real, is it contamination, is there another explanation.
